utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I thought we should bring something to the Chamber's attention. Apparently there's been some misunderstanding. We were informed on walking into the Chamber this morning that the Defence intends to call Mr. - it's a public witness, I think - Mr. Praljak as the next witness, which was not at all our understanding or intention. It's our understanding that the next witness would be the same order as was listed in their previous order, and we are not prepared to go forward with Mr. Praljak at this time. There was -- the issue last week was whether a certain document could be provided, could be unsealed, and it would depend -- also a factor was whether we would indeed be able to finish the first witness last week. Due to the Chamber's accommodations on Thursday afternoon, we were able to finish that witness on Thursday afternoon. We also were able to have the document -- previously sealed document unsealed. And my staff and I have gone forward since Thursday, preparing for the cross-examination of the second listed witness and are completely surprised this morning that, as the Defence has indicated, they will call Mr. Praljak instead. So we're not prepared to receive his evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe that it was last Wednesday when Your Honour requested the Defence counsel if we could have the second witness - due to the fact that the Prosecutor had filed a notice or a request with the Appeals Chamber and didn't know how long it would take to get that statement of that witness - if we could have him come at a later date, and we indicated to Your Honour that we could and we would call the next witness next. Because I think even Mr. Stringer indicated with the motion that he had filed with the Appeals Chamber, it was unclear as to when they would rule on that or when they would release that statement, and they did not want to cross-examine the second witness without it. So we went forward and called off that second witness from your ruling on Wednesday, last Wednesday, to finish the witness, first witness, on Thursday. We believe, Your Honour, that -- we understood what your question to Mr. Krsnik was, and that is that the second witness be called out of order so that the Prosecution would have the opportunity to have the statement in front of it for cross-examination. Your Honour, this witness, we cannot file anything before 9.00 a.m. because the Registrar does not open until 9.00. Last fall, when the trial started at 9.30, we could often make filings between 9.00 and 9.25, before we went to court. We have a notice that we intend to file today at the earliest possible time, simply notifying the Prosecution and this Honourable Trial Chamber that we are requesting additional time for Mr. Praljak. We had estimated 3.5 hours on direct examination. After our history with our first witness, we believe that we may have guesstimated that time wrong, so we're notifying both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution that for Mr. Praljak we would ask for five hours direct examination. We believe it's better to err on the side of telling the Trial Chamber more time than less time. Therefore, we believe that the Prosecution would not be in the position to cross-examine this witness until sometime tomorrow in any event. We believe there is no way we can finish this witness on direct examination today, even if the testimony only goes 3.75 hours or four hours, and we believe it might come closer to five. Thirdly, Your Honours, we have complied this morning with your ruling from last Wednesday, the 27th, wherein you requested and ordered that the Defence deliver to the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 67(A)(ii)(a), the information about any witnesses who might testify in regards to an alibi defence. Your Honours, we believe -- and I delivered that letter to Mr. Scott this morning. Actually, Mr. Stringer took it but I notified Mr. Scott that it was there. I know they have not had a chance to look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, would you please slow down for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Due to the ruling that you made, we went ahead and furnished the witness's name, whereabouts, what his testimony would be, and we also set out in that letter why we verily believe that, in fact, this is not an alibi witness. I don't know how to -- we have, because of the time limits involved and Rule 73(D)(i) on an interlocutory appeal, we only -- we believe we have only until the day is out to file that appeal on the ruling that was made pursuant to Rule 67. We obviously do not want to file an appeal if the matter can be rectified otherwise. Rule 73 does allow that if a Trial Chamber puts its ruling into writing and indicates it will give a written decision, then any time limit would be the seven days from the filing of the written decision. Again, we have -- and I would be happy to provide the Chamber with a copy of the letter that we sent the Prosecutor where we outlined why we believe there was confusion and there is no alibi witnesses, and we believe that the ruling will hamper and impede a fair procedure and trial for the accused should it stand. But in any event, Your Honours, I just wanted to bring that to your attention. We are in your hands. We can deliver a copy of that letter to you. But our time is running and we wanted to notify you of the fact that we may have misguessed on the amount of time necessary for this witness. We will try to sharpen our skills in that fashion. And, again, as far as my understanding, Mr. President, this discussion Wednesday was to have the second witness called off so the Prosecution could obtain the copy of his former filed statement in other case with the Appeals Chamber, so I don't know why there is any confusion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in looking -- in reflecting on the record and going back to the transcript, I think the word counsel just used is the correct word; there was discussion. There was never a ruling. The Chamber never indicated that, in fact, would be the schedule. There was open discussion about whether some possible alternatives might be pursued at that time. There was no indication that, in fact, that would be the course followed, and when no such ruling or further clarification was made by the end of the day on Thursday again, I and my staff spent most of the weekend not on holiday but working and working to prepare to meet the second listed witness. So we are not prepared to receive Mr. Praljak's -- we are not prepared to cross-examine Mr. Praljak. I suppose if they would like to call him and take his direct now, his cross-examination can be postponed if they have no other witness here today. We are not prepared, under any scenario -- it would be unfair to the Prosecution, unfair to the interests we represent, to the international community and to the victims in this case if we are required to prepare for cross-examination of a witness that we did not understand would be called today. Further, in terms of documents, Your Honours, I wish to make it further clear to Your Honour that we have not been provided -- apart from our own exhibits -- I have been provided this morning a letter listing 15 Prosecution numbered exhibits, which obviously we have. However, the letter goes on to say, "There will be other documents of the Defence, not yet translated, which will be identified through Praljak as well as tendering of the same." We have not received a listing of those documents. We have not received the documents themselves. We have not received any translations. We object to any of those documents coming into evidence by this Chamber's rulings, and if that's not clear, then we ask again for the Chamber to clarify its rulings on the exhibits because we have not been provided any exhibits for this witness except for the Prosecution's own exhibits, either translated or not. So we -- in addition to our objections to proceed with Mr. Praljak at this time on the basis of the schedule and the order of witnesses, we also object to the cross -- to the examination of Mr. Praljak at this time because the exhibits have not been properly provided to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik? How about those documents and exhibits? We understand that before the direct examinations, you have to furnish those documents you are going to use in your direct examination, which is quite different from the cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To start off with, good morning, Your Honours. And let me start off by saying that I don't know why this discussion is being held because I personally - and we can look at the transcript, turn the transcript back - I told the Court that Witness 3 would take the place of Witness 2, precisely so that the indictment -- that the Prosecution can prepare for Witness 2. And my colleagues asked for some unsealing of documents. I said that we will show full understanding. We were in similar situations and much worse situations than my colleague, so this was clearly stated on Thursday. I stated it in this very courtroom, and I don't understand why the Prosecution is protesting in this way. As far as the document is concerned, Your Honours, the Defence cannot be at a disadvantage. The documents have not been translated. We have invested superhuman efforts and translated the tapes ourselves into the Croatian language, into literary Croatian. We have supplied the translators in their booths with copies of those texts, and if they have the text before them, they will be able to follow the tapes. The documents have not, however, been translated. We wanted to pinpoint and identify those documents so that the Trial Chamber should know which documents they are and read them out. It's not a long list and the interpreters will help us, but unless that is done, we will have to postpone the proceedings. It is not your fault, it is not our fault, and it is not the Prosecution's fault, we all know that, but we have not received translated copies of the documents that we tendered last time, that we sent in for translation last year, in September, actually, of last year. But it is nobody's fault, and I know that nobody can be blamed. The translation unit and service has so much work to do and we understand that, but this cannot be a disadvantage for us. We cannot pay the price of that because those documents have not been translated. And now, if you curtail the right of the Defence to use them, that would be unfair. They receive a number, they have been sent to the translation service, and once they are translated provisionally, we will be able to go forward. And as we know, the witness isn't here every day. He's here today and then he'll leave, and the documents are linked to this witness. We have to take them together, witness and documents. And if the case is as it stands, we will have to ask for a postponement for the Defence to be fully prepared and then proceed according to the Rules or -- and the Prosecution is well aware of this. All the documents that we were able to furnish them with, we have done so up until today. And some documents that were in Croatian -- and my learned colleagues said that they could have them translated themselves. We gave them those documents too. So as I say, Your Honours, it's nobody's mistake. It's nobody's fault that we worked until 7.00 on Thursday, 7.00 p.m. on Thursday. You know that, in the meantime, nobody worked, and I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to check this out, but I know I'm not wrong because those are the words I uttered in this courtroom. I said that we would be replacing Witness 3 with Witness 2, my colleagues are informing me, and they have found it in the transcript. It is page -- in the record, it is page 8992, line 13-20. And it says in that part of the transcript -- that is to say, when I said what I said, you, Your Honours, said that we should bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there are several questions I would like to ask you, Mr. Krsnik. How many documents are you going to use through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you mean the documents that we haven't handed over yet? There are 14 -- rather, 15 of these, and in the letter to the Prosecution, we describe which those documents are. They are, for the most part, very short documents, comprising of just a few sentences, and 90 per cent of them relate to documents of the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia, which describe how many weapons were given to the BH army. I think that actually all the documents deal with that subject: the quantity, the date, and to whom these military materiel and equipment for the Bosnia-Herzegovina army were handed over to. We selected several examples from 1992 right until April 1993. Those are the documents. And not a single document, Your Honours, is longer than four sentences, with a list of the materiel and equipment which is enumerated in the form of lists. For example -- let me give you an example. The Defence Ministry of Republic of Croatia order for issuing materiel for the needs of the central rear base of Grude, to be placed at the disposal of the BiH army, Foca, Gorazde. And then it goes on to enumerate: ammunition, 7.62 times 39, et cetera, 13 million pieces, et cetera, 10, and so on. So there are 14 of those short documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you furnish those documents without translation to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and to the interpretation booths and the Prosecution. We did that today. Yes, today, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is the second witness available here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I do apologise, Your Honours. My colleague has just told me -- I have my headsets on. I'm listening to you, I'm listening to this, but my colleague informs me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, there's been a misunderstanding. My colleague gave the documents to the interpreters in the booths for interpretation purposes, but Mr. Meek was to have provided the Prosecution with the documents. He will do so. There was a misunderstanding. But yes, the next witness is ready and waiting to come in. Witness 2 has left, Your Honour. He left on Thursday, Witness 2. He was the protected witness under a pseudonym. I can't give you his name. He was to have been Witness 2 when we changed places. So we have Witness 3 here waiting today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more brief -- thank you, Your Honour. I should just like to inform the Court and my colleagues that Witness 4 has been taken ill, we have been informed. He was in hospital. So there will be another change in the order. Witness 5 will take the place of Witness 4, and he's on his way here. And unless that witness recovers, then Witness 6 will take Witness 5's place, and then Witness 4 will take the place of Witness 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I have to say that the Defence case is not well organised in terms of the documents and the witness list. I hope you could file us with a new order of the list of the witnesses so that we could know who will be the next and what's the change concerning all those witnesses. That's the first thing I want to say to you. Secondly, since we don't have much time to lose - as you understand, we only have four days this week - we will continue with the Witness 3 this morning and we'll give some time to the Prosecution for their cross-examination at a later stage, as we did in the Prosecution's case sometimes. Thirdly, I hope you could furnish the documents, even without translation, to the Prosecution side, and I will instruct the registrar to make those documents translated as soon as possible so that to guarantee the proceedings going smoothly. Fourthly, as for the alibi witnesses, Mr. Meek, I hope you could submit us with the letters you sent to the Prosecution, as well as the summaries of the testimony of that witness so that we could make a decision whether he's a witness of alibi or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will do that after the first break. Also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. President, I will do that at the first break. And what happened with the documents, they're in the translation booth. They got left in the translation booth, the copy for the Prosecutor, accidentally. If the usher could go to the translation booth and retrieve those, they can be turned over. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. Krsnik, we'll conduct our trial according to the time limit you submitted us according to 65 ter submissions. That is, this witness will take three and a half hours for the direct examination, not five hours. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But may I just say that we apologise you might have gained that impression. The Defence is well organised with respect to the witnesses, and we did prepare everything following your instructions, and we knew all this five days ago. It is just that Witness 2 and 3 were changed, and the Prosecution insisted on that and we adapted ourselves. And now the fact that we learnt about this next witness being taken ill, we have just learnt about that. But we will try and keep up the tempo, and I do apologise for having to say what I just said. I think that we did follow your guidelines and orders and the requests made by the Prosecution. Because Witness 2 was ready. He was here, present here, but not to lose time, he returned. I'm referring to Witness 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have made decisions already, Mr. Krsnik. So you have to submit a new list of order of witnesses. Usher, would you please call in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I will now give you just some short instructions. We speak the same language so I'd like to ask you to wait for my -- until the end of my question, and then answer, because of the interpreters, so that they could do their job properly. And so let us start, but just let us not forget that we need to break so as to facilitate the interpreters' work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, will you tell this Court, in a very few words, tell us who you are, what you are, what was your education, what did you do until 1990, what did you do until then, what did you do after that? Where were you, that is, which posts did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Praljak. I went to the secondary school at Siroki Brijeg for six years, and the last two years of my secondary school I did in Mostar. When I arrived in Zagreb, I enrolled in the electrical engineering faculty, and after eight terms, after eight semestral terms and my thesis, I graduated from it cum laude. And strangely enough, in parallel with the electrical engineering, I also studied philosophy and sociology, and I read them, and that was the condition then, so that I could then enroll the Academy for Theatre and Film Direction in Zagreb. So I graduated in philosophy -- from philosophy and sociology, and my thesis were the issues of ethics and freedom in Marxian philosophy. And following that, in 1972, I also graduated from the Academy for Dramatic Film and Theatre Arts in Zagreb. After that, I was -- I worked as a film, theatre and television director. In 1988 or 1999 [as translated], I joined the democratic developments in Croatia on the side of those Croats who wanted to put an end to Yugoslavia, such as it was, who wanted an autonomous Croatian state and who wanted to live in democracy. After -- following the attack of the Yugoslav People's Army and Chetniks from Serbia, and after the insurgence of Serbs in Croatia, I quit my political commitment, and in early September, 1991, as a volunteer, I went to Sunja, which is a small place near Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean in the Republic of Croatia, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia. Some 15 days later, I took over the command of the forces in the area, and that is where I stayed until March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Praljak. I think it will be better, because our time is very limited, perhaps it will be better for me to ask you questions and steer you through. So let me ask you, when did you go to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were you an officer in the Croatian army at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I went to Bosnia-Herzegovina around the 20th March, 1992, and I -- as an officer of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And was it your decision to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, tell us -- you didn't tell us where you were born. Perhaps you forgot that. Do you have any relatives, any siblings, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you do, where is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Capljina, and until the age of 18, I lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, my parents still lived in Mostar. My sister and her husband and two children were living in Sarajevo and teaching at the university, and I had also some other relations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? Can you tell us why was it that you left in March, not in some other -- not at some other time? Did something important happen which prompted you to do that? And did you go of your own will or was it an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, the war in Croatia was not over but it had calmed down, and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was just starting. My knowledge and the political -- of the political situation and the gist of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb aggression made it quite clear to me that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be more difficult and bloodier than in Croatia and that the weapons which had been moved from Slovenia and Croatia with, among other things, the help of the international community which had requested that the Yugoslav People's Army pull out its weapons to Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, will you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I will. So I'm still speaking about the international community. At that time, it was still unable to understand the principal reason of the war in the former Yugoslavia and therefore aware of two dangers, the breakthrough of the Serb forces -- of the Serb forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina, via Kupres and Livno to Split, and through the Neretva Valley to Ploce, and realising that it would completely disable the defence of the Republic of Croatia and seal the fate of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So my reasons of ethical nature, my duties and rights, the duties and rights of every man of integrity and every patriot, made me, for all those reasons, volunteer to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina and try to help with the organisation of the defence in the same manner in which I had done that in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever get an order, an official order, from the commanders of the Croatian army, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia, the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, that you or somebody else should go there to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: In line with my declaration that I will speak the truth before this Court, I affirm that neither I nor anyone else of whom I know, received -- nor in line with the decisions of the diet of the Republic of Croatia and the President of the state of the Republic of Croatia, who was -- who is at the same time the supreme commander, such an order was not issued because the order -- the decision was that the forces of the Republic of Croatia, that is, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, and under -- pursuant to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, these armed forces could not enter the territory of another state if -- unless a military pact had been concluded with such a state. Counsel, on two occasions during the war this was violated, and if you ask me when, then I will answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, we shall come to that later on, because I'm trying to restrict my questions because the time is limited. And now very briefly, Mr. Praljak, tell me, which events preceded -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which preceding events in Bosnia-Herzegovina confirmed the decision? Are you aware of the -- do you know what the country was -- what were the situation in Polog? Did it exist as a state, like Bosnia-Herzegovina -- like Slovenia, Republic of Croatia? Could you very briefly tell us what was the situation? That is, what you know of your own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I shall try to be very brief, although disintegration of states unfortunately necessitates analysis and these are measured by volumes and volumes of books, tomes of books filling up entire libraries. Yugoslavia disintegrated because it lost its raison d'etre. In Slovenia, the war which looked like a media crime, manoeuvre of a brigade, was over in a few days' time. The Serbs believed that with the disintegration of Yugoslavia, the internal boundaries between republics would no longer apply so that they adhered to their myth which was in force with them for over 150 years, since their famous programmatic declaration, the so-called Garasanin Project. And because of that, they thought that with the disintegration of Yugoslavia, they were entitled to a state whose borders they would conquer by military force. As regards Croatia, those borders were such that Croatia would be reduced to larger Zagreb territory, Karlobag, Virovitica. As for Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a series of documents which have become accessible today but of which we were unaware then, the Serbs believed, and all their political steps within their people in Bosnia-Herzegovina went in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the last few minutes, the witness has said several times -- talking about what the Serbs believed. No foundation has been shown for how this witness knows what the Serbs quote, "believed." I also object that this sounds an awful lot like expert opinion testimony. This witness has not been tendered as an expert. The Prosecution has not been provided with an expert report, as provided by the Rules, 21 days before the witness so testifies, and we would object to any evidence in the nature of expert opinion being given by this witness and also again object to the basis, the foundation, for his testimony, about what the Serbs believed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, Your Honours, the witness is testifying about his first-hand knowledge. I know that perhaps it is difficult to understand for my learned friend because he did not live with us at that time in the former Yugoslavia. What Mr. Praljak is telling us now are not expert views. These are views that we learnt about from elementary school to the university, and we lived in that system, and everybody who lived there and who went through that can testify about it. He is presenting his views. He is testifying about what he went through. He is not presenting any expert views. He is testifying about his own experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, what we want to hear is what you saw, what you did. That is the first-hand knowledge of the event. It is quite acceptable if you say what your knowledge is. But you should not quote what the others said or what the others believe. Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any personal knowledge about what happened in Polog and, after that, what happened in the village of Ravno, in Dubrovnik, in Sibenik, Vukovar? Can you tell the Court that? In the light of this, what is your personal knowledge about these things? Let us start first with Ravno -- no. Let us talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, I hope you will understand my wish to not go beyond facts. These are statements of Borislav Jovic, Garasanin, and these are all facts. But I will come back to Polog. What I am testifying about are Serbian units in the territory of the Republic of Croatia against whom I fought. What I testify about is the massacre of the wounded in Vukovar, the slaughter of the civilian population, the attacks on Zadar and Sibenik, shelling of Osijek, destruction of Dubrovnik, complete destruction of Dubrovnik. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it started in 1991, when the regularly invited reservists of Montenegrin and Serb ethnicity in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were legally [as interpreted] invited and the attack on the village of Ravno, which was razed to the ground and its population slain. On the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, there is a village of Uniste, which suffered the same fate, even before the village of Ravno. The Serbian tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army in the village of Polog, within reach of Siroki Brijeg, the tank-armoured brigade wishes to arrive in Kupres so that from there, through Livno, they could cut off Split. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a state, still in Yugoslavia at the time, even though multiparty parliamentary elections had already been held, does not have any power to prevent such plans of the attack this time against the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not see -- at least, I did not see any possible sign, either in the world or within the country, which at that time could or wanted to stop that war, which meant that I felt, both as a man and as a member of a people, and as a man of integrity, I felt it was my duty to go down there and place myself in the service of the defence. At that time, the tanks in Polog were stopped by the unarmed people, which next to those tanks sang songs, attesting to their desire for all this to be over, to be finished, without shedding blood, without war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was it then shown? Was it recorded and shown across Yugoslavia how these events developed in Polog?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. There are television and film records of all that, they were publicly broadcast, and many people have them in their personal databases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We do not have time to see this tape, because we must rush forward because of the limits of time imposed on us by the Court. Tell me, Witness: What about the state institutions at that time? And I'm referring to late 1991 and early 1992, before you went there. What about the state institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise. Of course, after you got there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I volunteered to go there as the commander of the zone operations around Mostar on the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was it like?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please hear what I have to say about this. None of the things that modern society understands a state or a civilised form of the existence of a society was not in existence there [as interpreted]. The attack on Sarajevo put an end to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a regulated form of state entity, which means no schools, no banks, no post offices, no shops, no police, no army, no supplies, no electricity, no water supply, no communication between cities and towns. It is zero regulation of a society. No sovereignty, no authority, no form of order was in existence there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what did the people do? How did they organise for this defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: People began to rally of their own will, and the zero degree of organisation started. That is, a certain number of people volunteered to undertake certain responsibilities to organise both formations and some form of organised life in the rear of the front lines, which at that time were largely set up against the Serbs. In the area in which I was, the primary task was to stop the Serb strategic breakthrough towards Ploce in Croatia, through the Neretva Valley, and from Kupres, through Livno, towards Split. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I will now show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And will the usher please help me. This is document EAC-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please read this document and tell us if Major General Ante Roso and Brigadier Miljenko Crnjac arrived there like you or in a different way or following orders? Well, read the order and then tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. Read it for yourself, because Their Honours have this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: So Major General Ante Roso and Brigadier Milenko Crnjac, with an "A" rather than an "E," became commanders of the zones of operations mentioned here, but General Janko Bobetko should not have had to write about it and had no reason to do that. We, because we went there of our own free will, and General Janko Bobetko did not command, did not issue orders concerning our activities there. Then the logical question is why did he write this? Janko Bobetko at the time was the commander of the southern front, of the southern theatre of operations, and in the Republic of Croatia this is the area from Split and Dubrovnik, which was imperilled, like the whole southern part of Croatia. And as he was of quite an advanced age - because he was in World War II. He was one of the first fighters on the side of the anti-fascist coalition - and in line with the patriarchal ethics and world view which exists down there, he liked to be what the Russians would call elders, elders to whom people -- whom people turned to for advice, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So he was not in command, nor was he able to command any units of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: That is right. Janko Bobetko did not command any units of the HVO. At this point in time - I don't know the exact date - but the commander was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, and that was General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the national composition of the army was that was being founded with respect to the area you were in, can we call it the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The composition of the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Witness. I apologise. You have the screen in front of you, so when you see that the typing and the interpretation has stopped, you can continue, carry on with what you were saying. That is a good indication.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The composition of the army of the Croatian Defence Council corresponded, with slight differences, to the ethnic composition upon which the unit was formed to begin with. In the area that I was commanding at that time, and that was the area from Capljina, north of Mostar, to Konjic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Witness? Can you tell me how you commanded? Did you have a rank of any kind? Did people have ranks at all? How did they accept you as commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, there were no ranks at that time. I have already explained to the Court that it was what we called the zero organisational level of a social organisation and, by the same token, army organisation. In other words, what I mean is that we were accepted exclusively on the basis of the sentiments and feelings that the people had towards certain people whom they had known previously and come to accept as commanders, and those people were -- those qualities were their ability to organise -- for example, their organisational skills, the authority they wielded in their presence, the certainty of their knowledge, and above all, the fact that we had come from Croatia with a great deal of war experience behind us already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness: Was it a joint defence? Were there any Muslims in the HVO units at that time? How was all this organised? Were you organised with them? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Defence at that time was wholly joint in character. The national composition or ethnic composition of the battalions, because they were smaller units in Mostar, roughly corresponded in full to the national composition of the population in the area that a battalion was set up, and this also applied to Livno, which is where General Roso was. So that according to the people, the list of persons who came to take up their uniforms, you can see that in the Croatian Defence Council there were units which were predominantly - which means more than 50 per cent - predominantly made up of Muslims, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for the usher's assistance to provide us with document EAC-13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you read it, please, first, Witness. Read it to yourself. Look through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should like to ask the Prosecutor to warn me if any of these documents are under seal - we did look through them, but just in case, we don't want to err - and then we can move into private session. We did look through all the documents, but if the Prosecution should notice that some of these documents are under seal, could they please let us know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If you've read the document, you see the date is the 18th of June, 1992, to the attention of Mr. Andabah [Realtime transcript read in error "Andabak."] and Mr. Jaganjac. Let me ask you first: Did this man with the surname Andabah exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andabah with an "H," for purposes of the transcript, please. Could it be reported as it says, not with a "K" but with an "H," A-n-d-a-b-a-h. Thank you. Andabah, with an "H" at the end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A short question: Was there somebody called -- or rather, with the second name Andabah?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about Andabak, with a "K"? And if so, do you know, was that one man or several?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: This here refers to Brigadier Andabak, with a "K."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So the surname is Andabak with a "K." Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, with a "K." During the war, I met three people called Andabak. This particular Andabak came after me, as commander of the zone of responsibility that I was talking about earlier on. And he was born in the area. He originated from there. Zdenko Andabak, that is another Andabak, he was commander of a unit of the military police, and I also met him on several occasions during the war. Then there was a third man with the surname Andabak. His first name was Ivan, Ivan Andabak, whom I met as commander of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who is Mr. Jaganjac? Tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jasin Jaganjac was a Muslim, an ethnic Muslim. He was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. At the beginning of the war in Croatia, he took off his uniform and came to fight on the side of the Croatian army against the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but were there many officers of that type who were officers of the HVO and were ethnic Muslims? And if so, did they return as officers of the HV in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a lot of people like that, somewhat fewer officers than fighters. There were more Muslim fighters than officers. But many of them fought in Croatia, although they had been born or lived on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The vast majority of these people at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina returned there for the simple reason that they wanted to defend their home, and that was a defence of their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean their own house? Is that what you mean when you say "home"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, their own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So Mr. Jaganjac was an officer of the HV, that is to say, the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, he was an officer of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, he was commander of the southern front, Janko Bobetko once again. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Jaganjac came down there precisely at the insistence of a few of us and at his own personal request to come to Mostar. He asked to come to Mostar in order to prevent any kind of expansion of the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in the territory, in the area, to stop a conflict from flaring up. That is my answer to your first question. As to your second question, let me say this: What this order issued by General Bobetko refers to is something which the army was to undertake after an operation in which the Croatian Defence Council freed first of all the right and after that the left bank of the River Neretva, in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We'll come to that later on, Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: And I led that operation, and thereby this document loses all meaning and sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We are just dealing with general questions by way of introduction and then we'll move on to the details and concrete events later on. Tell us, please, what your connection was and links were with the Republic of Croatia at that time. Did you have any links with the Republic of Croatia at all? Did Croatia help by way of weaponry or any other way? Could you tell us a little bit about that, the relationship there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I do apologise, Your Honour, but just looking at the clock, I don't know whether you wish to take a break, Your Honours. Is this an opportune moment or have you planned otherwise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll stop here and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please bring in the witness. Mr. Krsnik, this is a direct examination, so I hope you could inform us beforehand what kind of documents you are going to use during your direct examination so that we could be prepared and bring the right documents here. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have informed the Court. We handed in the list of documents that we shall be using.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I received the list but I received one copy, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise. I thought that we had submitted more copies. I do apologise, Madam Registrar, for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. We only received one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe during the break, we could have it copied and furnished to us. Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall certainly do so. Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let us remind ourselves, we left off with links with the Republic of Croatia. Let me ask you another question. Did you personally have contacts with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contacts with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question linked to the Republic of Croatia, this assistance in terms of weaponry, armaments, if we could go back to that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I've already said that partially in explaining my previous answer. The Republic of Croatia was not able -- or part of the Republic of Croatia, that is to say the Ministry of Defence, that part of it, and within the Ministry of Defence, the main headquarters of -- staff of the Republic of Croatia was not able to issue an order on the deployment and use of units of the Croatian army on the territory of another state. If any lower level commander were to do so, the unit and members of that unit had the right to refuse to carry out an order of that kind without suffering any consequences of a legal nature. And so, sir, I myself participated in a public television broadcast, a programme, together with the then Minister of Defence, who was Mr. Gojko Susak, we took part in the same programme, and the two of us explained to the Croatian public and especially Mr. Susak, Minister Susak, did, and stated loud and clear and logically and unequivocally confirmed the assertions and words I stated earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was, this television programme, when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was in 1992, might have been May or June of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now like to ask the technical booth to play the tape and with the supplement number 5, the transcript number 5. Could you just play the tape and I'll tell you when to stop. I have skipped over a few of them to save time so I'm referring to tape number 5. [In English] Exhibit number IDD 1/50E. [Interpretation] So Madam Registrar, this would be number IDD 1/50, exhibit number, and the interpreters have the transcript of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just for the record, we have no transcript in B/C/S or English, or certainly no translation of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, are there any translations of this tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said at the beginning that we have the text in Croatian, which we have handed round to the interpreters and the booths, and they will interpret it simultaneously on the basis of the written text in Croatian. We ask them to do that. But I have a copy for the Prosecution as well, in Croatian, so the translation will appear on the transcript, actually, as the tape is played.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps at least the B/C/S transcription could be provided to us at the same time it's provided to the booths, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please start the tape and I'll tell you where we shall begin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Review and promotion of the 9th Muslim Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the wrong tape. That is tape number 1, cassette number 1. I say this to the technical booth. We need number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a fast-forward, please? Fast-forward, please. Fast-forward and I'll tell you when to stop. Stop here briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Praljak: Was that the event in Polog?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this was the event in Polog. The people stopped the tanks. The President of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, arrived and the crowd greeted him with general ovations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fast-forward, please. Stop here. And may we rewind the tape to the beginning, please, of this particular scene. From here. Could you play the tape from this point, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] From Zagreb. "PRESENTER: If a Croatian soldier refuses to go to the front in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Derventa, for example, can he be punished as a deserter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: He can't. PRESENTER: I have received a group of questions from our viewers, which is not any one of you particularly."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence, Mr. Gojko Susak. "MR. SUSAK: The officers of the HV army have told us the conditions under which the HV can go to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are volunteers who were born in these territories or volunteers who wished to go to defend the territory, and that is the way in which we helped them. But there is no order which can be issued to order somebody to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we rewind the tape, please. Could you rewind the tape? And stop here. Stop here, please. Play the tape. May we see the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] From Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us where you are on the tape, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I am third from the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the other gentlemen taking part in the programme were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: First is the presenter; then we have Minister Susak; the third person is myself; number 4 is General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we have a date for this broadcast, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he does not remember the exact date, but the month was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th or -- was May or June 1992, thereabouts, May or June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The programme --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us who we have sitting round the table.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I reached General Lucic, who is number 4, the fourth man. Then we have three other gentlemen from the Defence Ministry who were well versed in subjects such as refugees and the care of refugees, financing, and so on, displaced persons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, if I put it to you, and if I tell you in this Trial Chamber that witnesses appeared in this Trial Chamber, in this courtroom, who claimed that the HV, the Croatian army, that is, was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in Herzegovina, all the time, and that it took part in operations with the HVO, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: My answer would be the following: I would say that that witness was lying. This broadcast, this programme, was organised precisely because of the need to clarify the constitution and the manner in which the units of the Croatian army, the HV, were sent, because the units -- and Derventa is mentioned here, Derventa. And this is the summer of 1992 that we're talking about, and it was when the Croatian and, in part, Muslim population from Posavina, part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the river Sava, was expelled and killed. And I can even enumerate some units which, although they were composed of people from the locality and the territory of the Republic of Croatia, they adhered to this position and refused to cross the Sava River into Bosnian and Herzegovinian territory and thereby prevent the massacre carried out by the Serbs in that area. In that way, having done so, the Serbs reached the river Sava, and then, for many months, fought and shot at Slavonski Brod with all the weaponry they had at their disposal --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you explain to us where Derventa and Slavonski Brod are.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod is in the Republic of Croatia and it is at the -- on the left bank of the Sava River; and across the river, the Sava River, is the boundary, the border in that part, between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I should just like to say and I'd like to have you know that according to the doctrine of warfare, faced with a situation of this kind, when one army - in this case it was the Serb army - were violating all international laws and shelled a town for months on end from the immediate vicinity on the territory of another state, the doctrine of war law provides for the fact that the state under attack has the right to refute the enemy even by crossing into the territory of another state, and this is what we call to enter the rear and in-depth tactically. Unfortunately, we didn't resort to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the early part of your testimony, you mentioned that on two occasions, conditionally speaking, violations took place. Will you please explain it? I'm not sure I understood you properly. You said that the HV was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they did go in on two occasions. Could you please explain that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct. On the 12th of December -- no. On the 12th of April - I'm sorry - 1992, two days after I arrived in Herzegovina and took over the command in the part that I already mentioned, I requested assistance from the Croatian army because those Serbs predominated there. That is, it was the regular Yugoslav People's Army, and opposite me, General Perisic. General Perisic was opposite me at that time. Later on, he became chief of the Main Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, and vice -- and Deputy Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, with a whole corps and all the power that a corps normally has at its disposal. The army that we were setting up actually came down to a number of groups of people who are wavering between the fear that they will suffer - they and their friends and their children will suffer the same fate as was suffered in Croatia - and complete disorganisation insofar as the establishment of an army was concerned. How difficult it is to put an organised army in place, I believe it is not necessary for me to explain. And at that time, I had the hole in my defence which did exist in some form and in a part right below a very small place in Herzegovina called Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please explain to the Honourable Court about Medjugorje. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Medjugorje is a small locality, holy place. It is known as the Virgin Mary's sanctuary. It is on the right bank of the Neretva, midway between Mostar and Capljina, approximately. After a -- following an agreement, a commander, I believe that he was a commander of a neighbouring Split, the commander of the brigade, when I asked him to, he issued a command, an order, and sent 164 men, and at that time it was called the Battalion, the 4th Battalion of the 4th Guard's Brigade in Split. And I mixed them up with domiciled units, with local units, to strengthen the defence, because the Yugoslav People's Army, commanded by General Perisic could otherwise cross -- take the road, the Medjugorje-Ljubuski-Makarska, Ljubuski-Virgora-Makarska. Makarska is on the coast in Croatia. And at that time, I personally was reprimanded for the first time by a clerk in the American embassy, Mr. Zorelis -- Zorelis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Z-o-r-e-l-i-s is how the witness pronounces it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him that we go together to inspect, in order to verify my allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which was the second instance, the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: As soon as we organised ourselves, that unit abandoned that position. The second instance, sir, was in 1993, autumn, early autumn; late summer/early autumn. We asked that the Croatian army extend its area of defence of Dubrovnik towards Stolac, a place which is some 20 kilometres east of Capljina, because in view of the narrow territory that the Republic of Croatia has in Dubrovnik, it is impossible to hold defence lines on the border itself. The border of Croatia above Dubrovnik is at a distance from which one can fire at Dubrovnik with a pistol. The Croatian army units were deployed as agreed in the area, but although this was a logical defence deployment of the Republic of Croatia, the American side filed a very forceful protest and the -- we -- the Croatian army pulled out those units and I set up the Technical Group II and took over those front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help us with a document. EAC-5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I will now give you five or six documents and I will ask you to read them all and tell us with which one of them are you familiar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I referred to this document, so this is the 4th Battalion, 164 men, who were, on the 12th of April, 1992, deployed under the order of the command of the 4th Guard Brigade, Mr. Mato Videk [phoen]. It was the first time when acting under the orders, one battalion, that is 164 men of the Croatian army, in the -- entered into the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Two questions: How long were they there? I don't know if that is in the transcript. And secondly, what was the political and legal situation on the 12th of April, 1992? Has Bosnia already been recognised? Can you comment on this regardless of the defence -- the defence of the territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised thereabouts, I believe it was after this date. So as regards Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was from the point of view of law, formally speaking, it was still a part of Yugoslavia, but in reality it was a -- the continuing year, year-and-a-half-long aggression of the Serb forces against primarily peoples, and then within peoples, these states which existed by law, formally speaking, following the disintegration of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The next document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I believe -- excuse me. I believe that this unit stayed there about a month or a month and a half, but I couldn't tell you the exact number of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document EAC-15. And -14, AEC-14, so the witness could comment on both of them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you will be shown another order so you can look at both of them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel Siljeg, Zeljko Siljeg, did not write accurately the sentence that the officers who have assigned to the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to join the Croat Defence Council cannot, without the authority of the Croatian Ministry of Defence, leave the territory. Such sentences are written out of despair, of a man made responsible to defend something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to that form of answer. The witness can say whether he disagrees with it for some reason, and assuming he has a personal foundation for believing this document to be inaccurate, but I submit that it's not a reasonable answer for him to respond in such a way he says, "Well, this person, this Mr. Siljeg, didn't know what he was talking about or he spoke improperly." I submit he's not in a position to know that. It's not a proper way to address the documents. Obviously, he wants to dismiss the documents, but I think he has to do it on some other basis besides saying that the person who wrote it did not know what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect for my learned friends, if they show a little bit more patience, they would hear why is the witness testifying, first-hand, about this. And then he would know that the colonel mentioned here was his immediate subordinate. They were together all the time. And he's a witness about this. He is not making things up. And besides, if you look at the list of witnesses, it is quite logical, and I also promised that every document will be shown and testified about by a person who signed it. So this same will hold true of this document. But -- of course. But Mr. Praljak was directly in that Main Staff and therefore he knows about what it is all about because this one here is directly subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I'm afraid you have to ask some questions to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you just heard what Their Honours have asked me to do, namely, whether the undersigned Colonel Siljeg was your subordinate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: He was subordinate to me whenever I was down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you know about this so-called, would-be order that he signed? Would it be in line with your orders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, it has no legal basis. It has the basis of a desperate man who is fighting with a fundamental problem on the ground and that is that the units are not organised in a manner in which an army should be organised in a state which is organised and which has had an army for 120 or 130 years. There was a large number of people who were leaving the front line and there was no way one could prevent people from quitting because there was no state coercion that would make them go to the front line, and it is all on a voluntary basis and therefore it fluctuates from one day to the other, and Mr. Siljeg, in my interpretation, does something so as to comply with his task and keep people there, but this has no legal basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you now look at the next order, a similar one. This is EAC-14, of the 5th October, 1992, signed by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It was practically the same thing, and that was to introduce some kind of order, minimum order, at least in the listing of those who were members of the units and who had come from the Republic of Croatia of their own volition. And counsel, you can see here that two commanders, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, interpret in a completely different way the order that they received to make some order, at least in the rosters of the HVO units. That is, in Blaskic's case, there is no mention of the sentence that we argued about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Madam Registrar, could we have document EAC-20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Whilst we are waiting for the document, can you tell us how many volunteers, citizens - conditionally speaking, citizens - in 1991, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, joined the war in Croatia and how many of them went back in 1992, if you have any figures, that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, in the Croatian army, the records were not kept on an ethnic basis. Had there been in the Croatian army -- no, to show that in the Croatian army there were people of Croat, Muslim, and Serb ethnicity. Personally, I had 17 Serbs in my unit in Sunja. But if I may take the liberty to make an approximate assessment, in which case I can say that a number of volunteers from Croatia in the Croat Defence Council, at least insofar as units on the ground were concerned, operative units, starting from Central Bosnia downward, never exceeded 700 or maybe 800 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And were they all people who had come to Croatia from Bosnia in 1991 and then went back to their homesteads, I mean to defend their homesteads, their hearths?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say all of them, but yes, I confirm that with certainty for about 90 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now would you be so kind as to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is of the 26th of November, 1992. For the record, to repeat, EAC-20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It is signed by the deputy commander of the OS headquarters, if this OS means anything to you, Zoran Covic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I know about orders of this nature because I also participated in a whole series, in a whole string of such orders. Namely, when volunteers from the Croatian army came to the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina, men did not remove the insignia of the units that they had fought with in the war in Croatia, and that created major difficulties for us down there, because representatives of the international community never stopped saying, having seen people with such insignia, that it was indeed the Croatian army down in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Regrettably, for several reasons - and these are new uniforms, new patches - major problems concerning the purchase, on the one hand, and on the other, all the guys who had fought in Croatia wanted to come wearing those insignia because they meant something more than those for whom the war was just beginning. Unfortunately, or fortunately, that is how it is, how things stand with all the armies. It is important to be and demonstrate that you belonged to some good, valiant, and courageous unit. It applies to the Marines, to the Foreign Legion, Blue Berets, Green, Red Berets, and so on and so forth. And we had to grapple with this problem throughout the war, for the duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now I will ask you to comment on three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to ask the registrar to -- Ms. Thompson for documents EAC-31, EAC-32 - they are very short documents - and then Exhibit P538. I believe this document is under seal, so we'll have to go into private session for that document. The EACs are not under seal. First EAC, which are not under seal. When we come to P538, then we'll have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, in the Republic of Croatia, did refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina have their organisations, their societies, their clubs across Croatia, and were they trying to help their homeland in every way they could? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. But the problem is broader than that. When the attack on Croatia began, the international community proclaimed an embargo on the import of arms for the whole of the former Yugoslavia, and as for the Croats and Muslims, it meant that they were left completely unarmed, opposing against a major force, as was the Yugoslav People's Army, which served only the Serbian interests. All the Croats the world over, Muslims, the diaspora which is scattered all over the world, they all placed all their energies - that includes financial energy as well - at the disposal to procure, in every way possible, to procure weapons and make them available to those who wanted to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but did the Croats in the diaspora, living in Canada, the United States, and so on and so forth, did they also come as volunteers? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them came as volunteers, but they all - and I can say now all, down to the last one - felt how unfair was this embargo, and that in the name of the lofty principle of the right to self-defence, they violated it by buying weapons and arming the people. I can testify to that. At that time, Croatia was taking care of over 400.000 Muslim refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they also exerted themselves to help with weapons if they could, and those who wanted to go back and fight, they went back and fought. But an overwhelming majority of Muslim combatants, then and later, and commanders, had their families accommodated safely in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about Croats? Will you look at this document. So Croat refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia. You have the document before you. Will you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: You're talking about some Uskoks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Konjic, Vukovar, Zagreb. Avenija Vukovar, Zagreb. That's the address.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Zagreb, in the Avenija Vukovar and the Velesajam, this was the headquarters of a large number of organisations which rallied Croats and Muslims alike, based on their place of origin, that is, the Croats and Muslims of Konjic, for example, of Zepce, of Gorazde, of Mostar. And in that way, they set up the units and collected all possible assistance, everything they needed that was necessary. And literally, in a country which had been disbanded, there was nothing. So it means that the volunteers from the area could be sent over, yes, and agreement that they would be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now go into private session, with the Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And now I have a series of questions. Do you know how the process of arming the BH army developed in 1992 and 1993? How did that process show itself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The arming of the army, or rather, the Muslim forces, which call themselves the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, evolved continuously throughout the whole war via the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, either by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- no, I mean Croatia, by Croatia, which means the defence ministry of the Republic of Croatia, or what they themselves succeeded in procuring, which means their own logistical units, who were scattered across the globe. All this was collected up on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and transported, in convoys, via the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the area controlled --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean the Republic of Croatia, I believe.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I meant across the territory of the Republic of Croatia and the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. And let me repeat: This was an ongoing process throughout the war on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was placed at the disposal of the Muslim forces, or rather, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One part was hidden in convoys of international humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, they are documents 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Two objections and a request for clarification. Again, I think we're painting now with far too broad a brush. Could we have the dates when these provisions were being provided to the Bosnian Muslim army? As the Chamber well knows, I think, at this point in the trial, it might be one thing to say that Muslims were armed and assisted during the early days of 1992 and fighting against the Serbs, and it would be quite something else, the Prosecution would submit, to say that they were being armed at the time that they were fighting each other in Mostar and Stolac and other places in the middle of 1993. The testimony that the witness has given over the last few minutes gives no indication as to dates, locations, which units, which units were assisted, in what way. Did they provide -- did they get towels and soap? Did they get bullets? Were they fighting against Croat units or were they fighting against Serb units? There's simply a complete lack of information to make this testimony assist anyone, including the Defence. So we object to that. Secondly, Your Honour, there's further clarification that's needed. It says that some of this, the last on line 17: "One part was hidden in convoys of international humanitarian aid." Was this a shipment from Croatia that was hidden in conveys of international humanitarian aid? Was it a shipment from someplace else? Which convoy? Which international humanitarian organisation is accused of doing this? Mr. President, we are, simply speaking, in extreme, broad generalities, and we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you may ask some specific questions to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, had the Prosecution shown a little more patience, we would be showing documents with dates and names. So may I ask my learned colleagues to show a little patience during the examination-in-chief, just as I did. I'm just pulling out IDD 1/51 to 54 documents, and the Prosecution has these documents, which includes dates, quantities and names. We were just about to show those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the sake of the records, you might ask some specific questions concerning the dates, the whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have selected 14 documents out of hundreds, by way of example. So could the usher please assist me. Not hundreds; there are thousands of documents of this type. If necessary, we shall collect them all and tender them all as exhibits, if need be.
