I have provided the witness with all 14 documents to speed the process up. The witness can read out the dates, the quantities and who gave what to whom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents says, "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence." That is the header, the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the document on the ELMO. [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: [In English] IDD 51. [Interpretation] The document is headed "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence," and it is titled, "Authorisation." 7.430 pairs of boots for the needs of the -- of Tuzla, the Armed Force of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The party taking over the goods are Rasim, Osman, Jusuf. They are all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The date of each document, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is the 7th of October, 1992. Once again, the Republic of Croatia, Defence Ministry, 10th of October, Order for the Issuance of Ammunition, 7.62, times 39, number of pieces, 6 million. A Lanzer RPG-7, ten pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you explain what "RPG" stands for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: RPG is a launcher, anti-aircraft launcher. RPG-7, 300. Mines, 82 millimetres, 480. Mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, five pieces. And it is signed by General Colonel Ivan Cermak, who was the main logistics person of the Croatian army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For the record, the IDD number, please, of the previous document? Each document, start off by giving the IDD number.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: [In English] 52. [Interpretation] Document IDD 1/53.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The date now, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The date is the 10th of October, 1992, Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, order, ammunition, 763 million pieces, similar specifications as in the last document. Once again, the signature is General Colonel Ivan Cermak, the chief logistics person of the Croatian army. Document IDD 1/54 is the next document, the date is the 10th of October, 1992, placed at the disposal of the central logistics base for the disposal of the BH army for Foca -- for the defence of Foca and Gorazde. Ammunition, 30 million pieces. Launchers, RPG-7 type launchers, ten pieces. Optic sights, 40 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you mean by "optics"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Optic sight for RPG-7 launchers. Equipment for the launchers, 40 pieces. Rockets for the RPG-7, the number of pieces there, 996. 82-millimetre mines, mortars, 1.998 pieces. Mortars, 82-millimetre, types, 20 pieces. Optic sights for mortars. A recoilless gun, 82-millimetre, I can't see the figure there. I think it is 70 or 40. Shells, 82-millimetre shells for recoilless guns, 450 pieces. AP SMG 762. They are automatic rifles, 2.000 of those. And equipment for automatic rifles, 2.000 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you find 1993 in the documents? Look at the dates, please, and find the year 1993. And I'm going to tender them into evidence later on once these documents have been translated. Would you read out the number of the document first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is the 15th of February, 1993. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the command of the 4th Corps, that is the corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in Mostar. The main staff of the HVO, to the attention of Mr. Bruno Stojic, who was the representative of the board of the Croatian Defence Council. And diesel fuel is requested, 100 tonnes of D-2 diesel fuel, 200 tonnes, and the D-2 diesel fuel, 200 tonnes again, for the different locations. The fuel is located in Ploce, which is a territory of the Republic of Croatia and a harbour. And the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH army was Mr. Arif Pasalic, and he signed the document. He is requesting that this fuel be okayed, although the conflict between the BH and the Muslims forces were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the fuel was going to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Ploce-Mostar, Ploce-Jablanica, Ploce-Konjic, exclusively for the purposes of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can we look at another 1993 document. Before we move on to the next document, do you know whether Mr. Arif Pasalic received that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Everything went through. Document IDD 1/60. This was the 27th of February, 1993, and the Republic of Croatia and the Defence Ministry, the Main Staff authorises Mr. Hasan Rizvic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: A Muslim. To transport RPG-22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Through which territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Through the territory of the Republic of Croatia and area under HVO control, to territory controlled by Muslim forces, RPG-22s, ten pieces; RPG-7s, two pieces; and mines for RPG-7s, 18 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: General Major Stipetic, Petar Stipetic, and then the deputy -- and I'm not quite sure deputy of the Main Staff, but today's Main Staff deputy of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, who in this -- who was in this Tribunal. This next document is IDD 1/61, Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, the 2nd of March, 1993, confirmation allowing the transport of equipment for the requirements of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mechanised special units, Sarajevo, in the Zagreb-Metkovic area, passage through Bosnia-Herzegovina, and both these towns are in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, Croatia. The drivers are Cavic, Sevudin, and Rizvic, Hasan. Both of these two men are Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the document is signed by?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: By the administration of SIS, the Security Service of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and Miroslav Medjimorec is the signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: This document is numbered IDD 1/62. The heading under the coat of arms is Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, the Security and Information Service, the administration. The date is the 15th of March, 1993. And this document states that in Visoko, for the requirements of the logistics centre in Visoko, actually, which is a place near Sarajevo and was always under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether the main logistics centre for the BH army was located in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, and it was one of the problems that we frequently insisted that arms be sent towards the jeopardised territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Gorazde, Srebrenica and so on, but according to our information, it ended up in the main logistics centre in Visoko and was ultimately used as weapons to attack the Croatian forces in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document specifies the vehicles and the drivers of those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, all the drivers were Muslims and we had 4.520 pairs of boots included, camouflage heavy coats, 4.820. And camouflage coats and camouflage trousers, 4.000, et cetera, and 400. And all the rest is illegible except for the signature, Mr. Josip Perkovic, who was, I'm almost certain, then the head of the Security Service within the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Next, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The number of the document is IDD 1/63.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of March, 1993. Once again, the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. We have the reference number, et cetera, and it issues an order for issuing materiel and equipment for the requirements of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the logistics base at Grude. The logistics base was Grude. And that was a logistics base belonging to the Croatian Defence Council. A RPG-7 launcher, 75 pieces, mines for the RPG-7 launcher, 7.600 pieces there. A laser remote device, 38 pieces. Launchers for S-2M, ten pieces. Missiles, rockets, TF8ATM, 188 pieces. Bullets, 762 times 39, 800.000 pieces. Automatic rifles of the 7.62 millimetre type, 75 pieces. Bullets of the 12.7 calibre, 21.500, PMA mines, 1.500 pieces. A device for testing launchers and the TF8 missile unit, two pieces and a complete set for launching and targeting anti-tank rockets, TF8, eight pieces of those. All drivers driving those vehicles, and there are seven of them, were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did they have their military booklet number recorded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who were the people responsible for taking over these materiel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Beslagic Emir of Sarajevo, Sabic Tarik and Juric Franjo, the last being a Croat, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about the rest?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This brings us to the last document, I believe.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: We could skip the next document and go over to this final one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you given us the dates, please? I think we have missed a document, skipped a document. Page 2. I saw a million bullets somewhere, the figure for the ammunition was 1 million, in that last document you read out. Could you turn to page 2 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same registration number, the same order, bullets for automatic 7.62 times 39 rifles, and a million pieces of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what is the date, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of March, the same date that was on the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who was the responsible person which person took over the equipment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The same people, they were all Muslim drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the location?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The location was Metkovic-Grude. And this was signed by the future logistics head of the Croatian army, and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and he was Colonel Vladimir Zagorec. Now we come to the last document, IDD/64.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you give us the date, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The date is the end of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you give us the exact date, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it is the 30th of March, 1993, an order from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, for the issuance of materiel and equipment for the purposes of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bullets of the 7.72 times 39 type, 3 million pieces, 19.600. AK-47s, 3.000 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What is an AK-47?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is it a semi-automatic or automatic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many pieces of those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3.000. Number 3 was a RPG-7 launcher, 180 pieces of those. Mines for the RPG-7, 4.240 of those. Rockets of the Majlutka type. It is a Russian-produced anti-tank rocket, 9 M, 14 M, 50 pieces of those. Trotil, in shells, 30.625 of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you explain what Trotil is, or Trotilion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is a semi-produce for the production of all explosive devices, used in the factories of Vitezit in Novi Travnik and Vitez, Braca as well, and in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And item number 7?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Item number 7 were medicines, 16 boxes of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, tell us who the responsible persons were and the drivers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The responsible persons were Seta Said in Sarajevo, which -- who appeared several times, and as escort to the convoy, Samir Lukvancic, and they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about the 13 drivers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: All 13 drivers were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are all their particulars recorded there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that, following your guidelines, this would be an opportune moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thousands of documents of this nature could be brought into the courtroom if the Trial Chamber requires them. There are thousands of documents like that and supplies to the BH army via the territory of the Republic of Croatia was ongoing, continuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you referring to the whole of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, to the whole of 1993 and 1994. There were difficulties, yes, but it was an ongoing process. This process was continuous and never ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. It's time for our break and we will resume afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid we have to break here. We will resume at 25 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting the taking of the witness's testimony, but I feel that in light of the scheduling issues that have been raised this morning, probably before we break today - and I'm happy to put it off until the end of today's session - if we could save some time so we could address further the scheduling matters. Just as a preview - or I'm in the Chamber's hands - what I understand the counsel to be telling us this morning, which again is completely new to us -- and I understand that things happen. It certainly happened in the Prosecution case as well. I'm not -- in that particular regard, I'm not throwing any stones. But it does create significant problems, obviously, for the Prosecution to prepare for these major witnesses. These are -- it's no secret for me to say that someone like Mr. Praljak, Mr. -- I don't want to say any other names because some of them are protected. The Court knows the names of some of these first few witnesses. These are not, without meaning to be discourteous to any witness, these are not minor fact witnesses. These are very substantial, what might be called policy or political witnesses. They are labour intensive for both sides to prepare. Now, we learned this morning that because of some other witness changes, that the witness who was set to be number 5 is now apparently, if I understand correctly, now set to be number 3, which could be called as early as -- well, theoretically, as early as tomorrow. Now, we have been operating on the assumption that with two four-day weeks and the limited court days that we have, that we wouldn't probably get to Witness 5, at the earliest, until the end of next week or possibly even the following week. Now we find ourselves in a situation he could be testifying as soon as tomorrow. Anyway, Your Honour, I said I wanted to preview that. We can do it at the end of today's session, if the Court allows some time. The Court may want to think about its position. But, Your Honours, the Prosecution just simply cannot be in a situation, we respectfully submit and ask, to be prepared to cross-examine two major witnesses within the next day or two, which is completely contrary to the order that's been presented to us up until this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I ask you when you will be ready for the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would think that we could start the cross-examination of this witness by -- well, let me back up. I'm assuming, although I know the Chamber has given Mr. Krsnik some definite time limits, but I'm assuming that the direct examination will go into tomorrow. I suspect that -- and with no offence intended, I suspect we won't finish today by 13.45. Therefore, the direct can be finished tomorrow. I think that in fairness, Your Honour, the cross of this witness could be commenced on Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Krsnik, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. Your Honours, you are well aware how the commission for victims and witnesses works. Our hands are tied up in many respects when it comes to bringing in witnesses, and the worst thing is that we cannot tell the witnesses when their turn will come. We simply are not able to do that. It happened last week, and we once again went through the transcript. On Thursday, we had the whole situation cleared up, at the request of our learned friends in the Prosecution. There is nothing new that Witness 3 is here instead of Witness 2. That was no news. The only new thing is that Witness 4 ended up in the hospital, but that was a force majeure. Nobody could foresee that. And to save the situation, not to be reprimanded by the Honourable Court because we do not have any witnesses, we brought the next witness, who will arrive tomorrow afternoon, just to try to go by your order. You have to understand, Your Honours, that there are so many restrictions surrounding us that we cannot act otherwise. And when we were in a same situation as the Prosecutor, because the Prosecutor didn't know -- the Prosecution knew that Mr. Praljak would be coming up. But I'm not trying now to cast stones at anyone because I respect this Prosecution team. But we have never been -- we had never been allowed to prepare for longer than one afternoon when we were faced with an identical situation during the Prosecution case, and I can quote examples. A witness arrived, the Defence was not ready, it happened twice, and we were allowed one afternoon to prepare our cross-examination. It was always one day. That is, one afternoon. And it can be easily corroborated. So I do not think that the Prosecution is more important or should be more privileged or anything than the Defence, with all the assistance that they have at their disposal. Had I one per cent of what the Prosecution has at his disposal, then -- but, of course, the Defence will abide by whatever decision you take. But one thing more, Your Honours: When we prepared this schedule, when we made this summary, we simply could not foresee, we could not know, how long it would take to go through documents and tapes. So, Your Honours, three and a half hours shall be my direct examination, but not the tapes because the tapes cannot be included in the three and a half hours allotted for this witness. And this holds true of every witness. You know I'm very honest, I always tell you the truth. We simply did not include the time needed to show the tapes in our calculations of the direct examination. And I hope you will bear this in mind if we run into problems. I have a great deal to ask this witness and we are looking now at the time, the time we spent today. Today it might take me more than one hour, and I'm quite sure that it will be of use to the Chamber, and, of course, the witness must be ready to answer all your questions, too. Tomorrow morning, I won't have any other witness, anyway, so that thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we quite understand it's very difficult to arrange the witnesses in good order. There is something happened always during the proceedings. And we have a long Easter weekend, as you understand. So Mr. Krsnik, you may continue to direct examine this witness until tomorrow, and if there is no witness available, we will stop there. And on Thursday, the Prosecution will cross-examine that witness, but right after that, we will come to the next witness. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I do think it is fair. And just let me check if I understood you well. Can I show two tapes today and then tomorrow we may have -- we may need another hour or two, tomorrow morning, because I do not have another witness in any case, so that perhaps we might spend another hour or two with this witness. Altogether, I think it adds up to about four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this is the exception. In your case, you should abide by the time prescribed in your 65 ter filings, that is, three hours and a half. Since we don't have the next witness, you may have a little bit longer time for this witness. Yes, it is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And before our break, the Prosecution asked a question that this witness claimed that one part was -- the witness claimed that one part was hidden in the convoys of international humanitarian aid, and I hope you could clear it up. Yes. Bring the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is coming, I just want to express -- say thank you for the Court's accommodation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, before I move on to my next subject, I think we owe the Honourable Court the answer to one question, and that was to the objection of my learned friend regarding convoys, that weapons were hidden in convoys, and I believe we owe an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mean convoys, humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I believe it had to do with your explanations about the armaments. So will you please clear -- make -- explain what you meant.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: International organisations throughout the international community, with regard to the armament of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, Muslim and Croat component in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the armament of this community ran counter to the decision on the embargo on the imports of weapons in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That is Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. With an incredible number of refugees, displaced persons, expelled people, in the territories of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, mainly from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, a very large number of humanitarian organisations acted from the Republic of Croatia. There were the Red Cross and Red Crescent, but they were also a number of those. There was a whole host of organisations under the auspices of the church, be it the Islamic religious institution or the Roman Catholic, and they were used -- the trucks or cars would have double bottoms, or in flour and perhaps other foodstuffs, weapons were hidden, and then they crossed over not only to Croatia but also went on to Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, we wanted to control it all in one way or another, and after all, it was our duty because international humanitarian convoys were not always checked, and then in those convoys, weapons would be found. I can testify first-hand that it did not produce much effect because the weapons usually ended at the point of destination, because as often as not, even if something like that would be found, then convoys would go on, and not only convoys with aid but including weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I believe that your answer is satisfactory -- well, I don't know whether it is satisfactory but it is an answer. Whether it is satisfactory, it is up to our learned friends to say. Let us now resume where we left off. I believe we were talking about armament and your last sentence was that it applied to 1993 and into 1994 and that one could also supply thousands of such documents corroborating this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I said that and I stand by it. I mean, if I may, a simple Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. look at the Bosnia-Herzegovina map, the deployment of the forces of the Serbs, Croats and Muslims, shows clearly that from no other side could the Muslims get their weapons except from the Croatian side or from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. When we come to the maps. And I already thought that perhaps the maps would be the easiest way to explain various things to the Honourable Court, and I will then seek your help to do that. Were you a witness or were you an actor in the events in the formation of the army? I believe we did not yet hear the answer. In the organisation, in the formation, do you have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you have an example to try to portray the picture, to try to give us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I really turn away from the microphone, but it's so difficult for me. I cannot keep my head like that, and I also want to look at you because I have to show you the respect, and I also have to look at the witness, and it's all very awkward, and I'm very sorry but I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the interpreters cannot hear the counsel when he speaks out of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we imagine that Rotterdam was conquered and everybody was expelled, that it had no connection with Amsterdam, that they had no banks or police, all communications cut off, no electricity, no water, no judiciary, no police, no nothing, so that was the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in particular because it is made up of three peoples, and all the state structures were made up of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you personally, were you ever in a situation to have to use your authority or your own weapons in order to organise those self-organised guys, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I hardly had anything else at my disposal. I, as a commander, I participated in the liberation of the barracks in Capljina. That barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you give us the year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: 1992, after the proclamation and the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, a part of the international community, and then immediately afterwards by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know how it was recognised? What kind of recognition was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as a state whose boundaries were defined by Badinter's Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about their political order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The interpreters are far behind you. You have to remember that whatever you said will be translated into the other two languages. You have plenty of time, I can assure you. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again, Your Honour. Thank you for the warning. Yes, I wrote it down for me: Go slow. But Mr. Praljak, you should also look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Mr. Krsnik, and I will answer slowly all your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This time it was my fault. I'm not blaming you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, what about the rest? What about the internal political order in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I do know. Unfortunately, or fortunately, I also took part in most of these talks following the referendum which was organised at the request of Badinter's Commission and in which the Croats and the Muslims voted for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, that state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is, their external -- their state borders were recognised. But the notion of a state or its sovereignty was simply non-existent there. And the evolution of the war and all that happened in the war and why the war started and why the war went on, behind all this is the fact that during those years, with the help of the international community, the participation of the Muslim and Croatia in those talks, attempts were made over and over again how to end the war, how to find a solution for the internal order of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, from the very beginning, the Serbs refused any possible Bosnia and Herzegovina which would not be within Yugoslavia. That was their fundamental premise. If Bosnia and Herzegovina leaves the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia, then the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina will take out a part of its territory into the Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, will secede and will not recognise that state. That piece that they wanted to take was between 66 to 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What will you say if they were -- if that there were witnesses here who said that Croatia wanted the same thing, or rather, that the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to do the same, that is, secede its part of the territory and annex it to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I would answer to that that of course there was some thinking along those lines. There were some ideas. But political and -- the political activities and the state of the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia never did anything to support any such thesis. This thesis can be easily developed ad absurdum. That is, a state which wants to secede a part of the territory of another state in which the same people lives would be the first one not to recognise such a state, that is, its territorial integrity. It wouldn't, prior to that, use all its persuasive powers before that to talk the people of the neighbouring state to participate in the referendum and say yes and opt for the integral state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had the Croat people not said yes in the referendum, yes for such a state, then Badinter's Commission would not have recognised the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina such as it existed in the socialist Yugoslavia because it would not have won majority, simple majority. During a major part of the war, the Republic of Croatia took care of up to 400.000 refugees. I'm talking about the largest possible number, people expelled from the Republic of Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia. The majority of these refugees were Muslims. The Republic of Croatia armed, trained, and helped the formation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the conflict with Croats in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I have to interrupt you because you are confusing this, and I must not do this. You mean Croatia? Because I hear you. You mean Croatia but you say Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, throughout the war, the Republic of Croatia, even before the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council, trained, armed, equipped members of the Muslim forces equitably, without ever raising any questions. It took care of the wounded in all the hospitals in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that is, Split, Karlovac, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you personally, do you know how many wounded were treated -- how many wounded members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were treated in Croatia, and do you know the years?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm afraid my answer will be inaccurate if I give you some figures. I mean, figures are mathematics and therefore need to be precise. But it must be -- can't be less than dozens of thousands during the war in the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When you say during the war, when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, from the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina - let us say that the beginning of the conflict was the attack on the Croat village of Ravno in Herzegovina - and at the end of the war, and we can take the Dayton Accords as the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now we've really made a very large detour from Capljina, and we were --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: You want me to describe an event. Well, fire was opened on that locality from both sides: from the left bank of the Neretva, where General Perisic's forces were, and from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how far is your parental home from Capljina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fifty metres. And when we took the barracks, we captured 33 recruits, conscripts of the Yugoslav People's Army. They were of different ethnic origin. They were Serbs, they were Muslims, they were Hungarians, and I believe there was a Slovenian or two. And when you have a situation like that, when it would be over, groups of people would emerge from time to time and they would start putting the place in the order as they seemed fit, and putting the world into an order as they seemed fit was that such prisoners should be killed because somebody -- because one of theirs had already been killed, whether it was a Serb who was killed by a shell or in some other way. And the only way, the only way then to prevent such a crime was the personal attitude, which meant that you had to cock your rifle and give a demonstration of enough energy and strength and courage to, even at the cost of fire, that is, at a loss of one's own life, to defend or prevent a crime. And although I was a commander, I had nobody from the state structures to call to do that, to intercede. So I can testify that then, and later, on at least 20 different occasions, I had to do the same thing. Unfortunately, police or secret police did not exist, so one couldn't go to them and tell them, "These are people who tried to commit a crime, so take them in." Because there were no prisons. There was nothing. All those men, all the prisoners from these barracks, are safe and sound and they all went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. Just -- I was talking to my colleague, the President, and it's not always easy to understand what's being translated. That doesn't make sense. If you look at it, Mr. Krsnik, in English, and go back on it again, and possibly the way we'll get around it with the translation is if you allow General Praljak to stop and then explain. Is he trying to say that after the attack on Ravno, that his soldiers took prisoners? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll attempt to have Mr. Praljak to explain this, because the Defence considers it to be important. This took place after the taking over of the barracks in Capljina, and it is 50 metres away from the gentleman's house. It was a barracks in which the members of the JNA were put up in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Who took the barracks? Who are the protagonists? Who was the victor? Who took the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have heard the Judge.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The place is called Capljina and it is in Herzegovina, 35 kilometres south of Mostar. It was the spring of 1992. Bosnia-Herzegovina was a recognised state. On the left bank of the river Neretva and on the right bank of the Neretva were Serb units, the forces of a corps under the command of General Perisic. The talks -- the discussion about leaving the barracks guaranteeing the officers the right to take their pistols with them, their small arms with them, that was -- but in view of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a recognised state, they couldn't take the weaponry and armaments from that warehouse with them. But General Perisic refused those terms. The Croatian Defence Council, under my command, on that territory, liberated the barracks in Capljina, and when it did so, what it found there was the following: 32 or 33 soldiers belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army who were recruits. They were young men who had been recruited. They were conscripts from all over Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia. They returned home safely, but in order to save their lives from individuals' desire to retaliate outside the law, that could only be stopped in one way. This retaliation could only be prevented in one way, and that is the weapons that they would have seized, that the other side had to seize weapons too. There was nothing that we could refer to as a civilised, organised --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I don't think that Their Honours will understand again. Perhaps they don't understand you because of the translation. Now, when you say that some people resorted to arms, they resorted to arms and lifted their arms against whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The soldiers in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And to prevent them, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I had to take up arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you cocked your weapons at those people - we don't know who they are, or rather, we do know who they are - is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. The possibility of taking these people into detention and arresting them was completely impossible. We weren't able to do that. There was no form of what we call an organised, civilised society. That is to say, there was no police, no legal authorities, nothing. One of those soldiers, Dr. Moro, he was a Serb, he was in the HVO and became a major in the HVO and was in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: General Praljak, I may be being stupid, but you see words are being translated as "they" and we don't know who "they" are. Were you in charge of an HVO unit which took over a former Serbian army barracks and then, whereas you guaranteed safe return and conduct for the 30-something conscripts who were found there, you said that you couldn't guarantee that they would be well-treated by "them" or "they." Who were the "they"? Were they your troops or were they the general population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, it is true that I guaranteed -- I guaranteed the safety of the soldiers that I took into custody, took prisoner, from the people that usually come in afterwards to pilfer and take revenge, and there were people of that kind who were ready to do so. I should like to say that there is nothing in the concept of unit -- and when I say "unit," I mean myself there and my endeavour to prevent a crime from taking place. A bus, for example, in which they were, on board which they were, could have passed by along a road, for example, without an escort, and somebody -- somebody might shell that bus or shoot at it, target it, in order to take revenge for somebody who had been killed by Serb shelling. The possibility of controlling the situation and preventing this kind of thing from taking place was very slight. We had to invest a great deal of energy and effort to organise society in order to have the minimum degree of civilised behaviour prevail. And we were partially successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you want to say that at that time, you cocked your own weapons, and using this force, you drove away those people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, and I did so on two occasions under circumstances of that kind. I was forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you could have been killed yourself, depending on who was fastest on the draw?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in 1992, how long did you stay on in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Formally and legally, I remained commander of that part of the battleground for about a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean while you were doing your organising there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I made endless attempts to organise forms of social, civilised life and conduct. Not because the people were uncivilised in any way but because the institutions themselves had crumbled. They had ceased to exist within 24 hours, the central authorities and everything else that goes to make a civilised form of social life. But afterwards, I would go as often as the situation required and as often as I was able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you take part in the war which was still going on with the JNA, or rather, the Serbs, in Mostar? And if so, what was your role there in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the end of May, 1992, I returned. I went back down there. Although I was not officially appointed to a command position, I did in fact exercise command. And in an operation there, I was together with Mr. Mladen Naletilic when we liberated Mostar, the operation to liberate Orlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What were the Muslim -- what was the Muslims' conduct like in Mostar during the war, the war against the JNA, at the time, that was being waged in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, once again, for reasons that can be explained, the Muslims were far more passive and far less ready to defend themselves from a Serb attack, the reason for this being that their political leadership, throughout that time, endeavoured to reach an agreement of some kind which would prevent the war. They hoped -- it is a good thing to seek negotiation and agreement, but it was more than clear, and said a thousand times, that it was the Serb goal to wage war. The Croats had already seen what a war looked like in Croatia. They witnessed the crimes that were committed in Croatia, both in Vukovar, in Skabrnja, in Zadar, and in Dubrovnik, Skabrnja, Skabrnja, Zadar, Sibenik, Dubrovnik, Slavonski Brod, and so on and so forth. And they knew full well that if -- unless they organised their own defence, they would suffer the same fate. For that reason, in their psychological preparation for war, and in the organisation they undertook, they were far ahead of the Muslims in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you personally have any contacts with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the then presiding officer in the Presidency, as a collective head of state, functioning as a collective head of state? Did you have talks, meetings, negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what he -- what position he took in your talks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: During the first meetings, he was still convinced that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be able to avoid the tragic fate that befell Croatia, that the Yugoslav People's Army would choose Bosnia as its domicile locality, and that the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as he referred to them, because of a mixed population, would not go to war against each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Please do accept my apologies. When you -- Mr. Izetbegovic said the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which people was he referring to in your talks, when you talked to him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: He was thinking, at the time, the Serbs, Croats and Muslims. Those are the people. He didn't distinguish between them and divide them up. He meant the population, the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, with all the three constituent parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many meetings did you actually have with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Until the end of the war, I think seven times in Sarajevo. We met seven times. And he claimed at the time that the war in Croatia was not their war, that is to say was not Bosnia-Herzegovina's war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What did that mean? What did that mean for the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that position, statement, of his?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Krsnik, it was like this. When somebody within a country, which considers itself to be a sovereign country, attacks two Croatian villages, Ravno and the other one, and destroys them and razes them to the ground and kills the people, and the first among equals in the Presidency, the primus inter pares of the Presidency, states that it is not their war, then there is a fundamental lack of understanding and lack of trust and confidence that a policy of that kind will be able to save people's lives and to ensure the survival of the people living in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In Zagreb, Mostar and Sarajevo, the delegations of Croatia and Bosnia and the meetings with the Muslims, how often were they? How often did they take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Up until the end of 1992, there were hundreds of meetings of that kind. They took place all the time. They were regular meetings, for example, in Zagreb, and Split, and in Mostar and in Central Bosnia as well. And incidents would occur in different places, and after each of those incidents, people would sit down to the negotiating table and try to analyse the situation, why the incident had taken place, and how to prevent an escalation of the conflict further. Meetings with the Croatian leadership were also frequent. There were tens of those, too. And a lot has been written about them. Articles have been published about that subject. It would be difficult to go into all of that here and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you explain to the Trial Chamber and all of us, could you help us gain an impression of these war zones and Bosnia-Herzegovina? And I'm going to show you some maps which might assist you in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a provisional number D1/65, IDD 1/65 is the number, and then 66, 67, 68 and 69. And may I ask the usher to give the witness the maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please take a look at the maps. They have been set out in a logical sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, if it is not difficult for you, Mr. Praljak, would you please read out all that it says in Croatian? Because it is not translated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: "Part of the strategic, aggressive, offensive operation in the aggression against Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And these arrows are pointing at what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: These are plans for the attacks, and that is how the attacks did indeed take place, in the Croatian territory of Baranja, from the direction of the Drina, against the Croatian territory of Slavonia, and then liberated -- in the liberating operation Biljeserk [phoen] and Donbanja [phoen] and Kordun in Croatia, and the Knin Corps, which was attacking towards Zadar and Sibenik. This here is the direction of the attack from Kupres field via Livno against Split, and through the Neretva valley towards Ploce. This attack was prevented, hampered and then prevented when the Livensko-Tomislavgrad front line was set up, was established, by the HVO in 1992, at the time of major attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, map number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: So January to March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please read the main idea.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: "The operative evolution -- development of the JNA for the first segment of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." These here are the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb volunteer units in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in March, 1992. The 4th Corps in Sarajevo, under the command of Major General Vojislav Djurdjevac. The 5th Corps in Banja Luka, Major General Vladimir Vukovic. The 9th Corps, Glamoc, Kupres, Grahovo, Major General Sava Kovacevic. The 10th Corps, West Bosnia, Commander, Major General Spiro Vinkovic. The 13th Corps in Herzegovina, made up of the Yugoslav People's Army, volunteer Serb forces from East Herzegovina and reservists from Montenegro, their commander, Major General Momcilo Perisic. And the 17th Corps in Tuzla, with its commander Lieutenant Colonel General -- one-star General Sava Janovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this was the deployment of the forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This was the deployment of the forces prior to the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and after its recognition, and it was against this enemy that we had to organise a defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this was the Defence Exhibit D66 -- no, sorry, IDD 1/66. The next map, please. This is IDD 1/67.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The occupied parts of the Republic of Croatia alongside borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The occupied parts are East Slavonia and Baranja, West Slavonia, Knin, and the Banovina of the Republic of Croatia. That's the name of the territory here. What is missing here, counsel, is the occupied part of the southern part of Croatia, up to Dubrovnik and behind Dubrovnik, up to Ston.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So it should all be in red, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. So from the legal point of view, from the legal point of view, formally, if we are treating this war as a war between the states, then Croatia was attacked by Bosnia-Herzegovina along several strategic directions. But this was the war between peoples and not a war between states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next map, please. This is IDD 1/68.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: This map dates back to April, 1992, and it shows the situation in the theatre of operations. That is the actual state of the front lines. Blue is the HVO, or rather, the defence lines of the Croat Defence Council. Green marks the Muslim forces, called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And red is the Army of Republika Srpska. These arrows here point at the defence, and these arrows, like this one here, mean the attack. In the western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is around Bihac, there is an enclave which is defended jointly by Muslim forces, majority, and Croat forces, that is an HVO brigade, with General Santic, who was killed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did they successfully defend it until 1995? Did they defend it together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, it had shrunk meanwhile to only a few kilometres around Bihac. And then the Croat forces, the HVO and HV forces -- that is, at that time, the international community allowed, and it was a lawful operation, the storm all -- then liberated all of the whole of this territory and arrived at the threshold, at the gate of Banja Luka, and then at the request of Banja Luka, they stopped. Sarajevo is besieged, Gorazde is besieged, and this here should be Srebrenica, which is also besieged. Later on, these will become the places of horrific genocide against the Muslim people. You see that this is basically grouped according to the ethnic composition of the population. The principal directions of the attack of the Serb forces were via Livno, Kupres-Livno, so that they could come out at Split and push back the Croat Defence Council and come to Ploce, which would mean cutting off completely the very narrow and almost indefensible part of the territory of the Republic of Croatia around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, and this blue in Central Bosnia, are these are the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: These are the enclaves of the Croat Defence Council. You can see Travnik and Busovaca, and Zepce should be here. Zepce should be here, Jajce, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was Jajce conquered nevertheless by the army of Republika Srpska later on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1992 the enclave of Jajce was very poorly defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But was the defence -- were there attempts to prevent its defence? Are you personally aware that it was the first, if I may call it that, incident with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when the reinforcement for the defence of Jajce arrived? Are you personally aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: The situation between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council in Jajce, except that it wasn't particularly good, is not something that I have personal knowledge of. But what I can testify about is that I, with the others, organised a unit of an army which was called HOS, H-O-S. At that time, those units were tolerated, like many others, even if they did not make part of the Croat Defence Council or part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One such unit, some 250 to 300 strong, before the fall of Jajce, was armed by us and fully equipped by us, in the Capljina barracks that I mentioned about when General Perisic's forces were defeated, and we sent that unit as a reinforcement to Jajce. More than 60 per cent of that unit's strength were ethnic Muslims. At that time, the tension in this area here, the tension between Croats and Muslims, unfortunately, had reached already such a degree, had become so intensive, that that unit riding buses never made it to Jajce. It was stopped in Muslim villages, although, and I repeat that 60 per cent of the men in this unit were of Muslim origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think we're at another area where a date would be helpful as to the attack on Jajce and when it fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Clear it up for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, will you give us the date, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, it was autumn of 1992. I wouldn't really be able to pin down the date, but if you want me, I'll try to dig it up from somewhere. I could bring tomorrow the exact date. But it was the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you now please be so kind and look at the next map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: I wish to mention merely that after the fall of Jajce, I went to Central Bosnia, and there, together with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and General Tihomir Blaskic, I organised there the defence in front of Travnik so as to prevent the Serb forces from taking the Lasva Valley and reaching Sarajevo. At that time it looked more than a probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit ID D1/69.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this was the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This was the situation in April 1992. And I want to show that in this part where I arrived, Mostar was practically encircled by Serb forces. Both Croats and Muslims were expelled from Stolac and we accommodated both groups in Medjugorje and tried to incorporate them in an organised defence. The Serb forces were on the right bank of the Neretva and we were threatened with a complete route of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, if I may interrupt you. We heard here witnesses who said that the Croats betrayed and surrendered [indiscernible] Stolac to the JNA. That is that we surrendered Stolac to the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, that we betrayed the Muslim people and left them at the mercy of those others -- at the mercy of the JNA. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I would call such a statement a blatant lie, a shameless lie. The truth is, for reasons that I mentioned earlier, that the Stolac Muslims welcomed the JNA troops there with flowers, that they prevented the Croat Defence Council from digging the trenches in the territories, in the property which belonged to them. The Muslims were confident at the time that in that way they would be able to avoid war and the very bad fate. Such a contact of the Muslims then entailed major consequences for the armies of both peoples in the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, again we seem to have a recurring problem with getting specification of date, and for these purposes, dates are important. So I would ask what date, what particular date or circumstance is he talking about now in connection with Stolac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- Your Honours, I'm -- the witness need not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you remember the months and years and all that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no, no. I know this, what I just told you about. Stolac refers to the period before April 1992, that is, March and early April, the beginning of April 1992. And I arrived there on the 10th of April, 1992. And several months later -- and several months after that, we were receiving Muslims fled from the area of Stolac and tried to accommodate them in every way possible. And they resorted to all sorts of devices to cross the Neretva, with our assistance, and as I personally participated in those, I can describe that down to the minutest detail and show -- and point at the houses and the whole tourist village owned by a Slovenian travel agency, where we accommodated those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the town was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I think we are coming to the end of the session, so my last question is: Did the HVO eventually liberate Stolac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In the end of May and in early June, the Croat Defence Council, in the joint struggle then with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but a small number of soldiers who took part in the operations -- I mean, a small number of Muslims took part in this combat, liberated both Stolac and the Neretva Valley and Mostar, and I personally commanded the action of the liberation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that we have come to the end of today's session, and I would therefore -- and that would be my last question for the day. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. I'm afraid we have to keep you here in The Hague for two or three days, and all you have to remember that you are still under the oath during that period. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. We will see you tomorrow morning. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will abide by the instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
